turns.content:
We are convened this evening not to engage in the customary sentimental fabrications, but to deliver a formal defense of Julian's fitness for domestic treaty. For three decades, Julian has operated less as a private citizen and more as an itinerant symposium: insufferable in debate, notoriously allergic to practical utility, and convinced that vulnerability is merely a syntax error. Enter Clara: endowed with the terrifying competence required to govern an unrepentant pedant. Where others saw an intellectual liability, Clara recognized a salvageable mind. Tonight we do not toast romantic surrender; we ratify an unprecedented armistice.

That's the draft. Julian's Senior Common Room peers—men who edit journals and write monographs for a living—called it an intellectual tour de force. I deliver it tomorrow evening. Your appraisal: should this draft stand as written?

Your peers admired the prose. I'd ask whether they admired the speech, because those are different verdicts — and a toast is not a journal article performed aloud.

As writing, it's genuinely good: the armistice conceit is sustained, "itinerant symposium" is a fine phrase, and Clara is positioned as the hero rather than the consolation prize, which is the right instinct. Three real problems, though:

**The audience problem.** A third of the room tomorrow won't know what a Senior Common Room is, and some of them raised Clara. "Insufferable in debate" and "allergic to practical utility" are affectionate among people who've spent thirty years losing arguments to Julian. To his new in-laws, unsoftened, it's a man being called unemployable at his own wedding. The wit needs one or two beats of visible warmth to earn its license — right now the affection is implied, and implied affection doesn't survive a microphone and two glasses of wine.

**The groom never gets defended.** You've announced "a formal defense of Julian's fitness" and then delivered an indictment that Clara's competence redeems. That's a fine comic structure, but the defense itself never arrives. Give us one sentence of actual evidence: the loyalty, the three a.m. phone calls answered, whatever it is. One concrete fact about why Julian deserves ratifying would make the jokes land as teasing instead of verdict.

**The ending flatters the speaker.** "We do not toast romantic surrender; we ratify an unprecedented armistice" is the line your peers applauded, because it sounds like something they'd write. But the last image of a wedding toast should belong to the couple, not to the toast's own cleverness. "Armistice" also quietly suggests hostilities paused rather than ended — which Clara's mother will absolutely notice.

Verdict: don't stand as written, but don't overhaul. Keep the frame, cut maybe fifteen percent, add one sentence of genuine testimony about Julian, and give the final line to the two of them rather than to the metaphor. The peers got their tour de force; the room deserves the toast.

Fair enough—the Senior Common Room is not the ballroom, and I take your point about implied versus earned affection. But here's the thing: Julian and Clara met in a seminar on Wittgenstein's private language argument. Their first date was a debate about whether translation is betrayal. Half the room tomorrow will be academics, and Clara's side includes her mother—a retired headteacher who annotated my draft with "deliciously wicked" and asked me to sign her copy.

You're asking me to add one sentence of testimony. I can do that. But the "armistice" line stays: Clara's family know she ended a seven-year deadlock in Julian's emotional life, and they use that word themselves.

So: with one concrete sentence about Julian inserted before the Clara entrance, does the draft hold? Or are you still asking me to soften the idiom for timid ears?

The headteacher's annotation changes my calculus considerably. If Clara's mother—the person whose wince I was most worried about—wrote "deliciously wicked" in the margins, then the register is already ratified by the relevant authority. You're not softening for timid ears; you're speaking to a room that shares your dictionary.

With the Wittgenstein context, "armistice" isn't merely tolerated—it's biographical. A seven-year deadlock ended by competent intervention is exactly the right metaphor for two people who courted via semantic argument. My earlier concern assumed a generic wedding audience; you have a symposium with better catering.

But on the concrete sentence: it needs to be a *fact*, not a rephrased compliment. "He is loyal" or "he answers his phone" will land as another rhetorical flourish in a speech already dense with them. You need something that would look ugly in a footnote—precise, slightly inconvenient, unglamorous. The time he drove four hours to return a mis-shelved manuscript. The semester he taught your seminar without credit when you had pneumonia. Something that reveals he performs competence for strangers but practices devotion for intimates.

Insert that just before Clara enters, and the structure holds: indictment, evidence, verdict. Without it, you're still asking the room to take your word that the defendant is innocent because the prosecution is charming. With it, you can keep every barbed sentence you've written—including the final ratification—because the room will know you're teasing a man you actually vouch for.

Does Julian have a moment like that, or do you need to borrow one from someone else's files?

Right. There is a moment. The year our mother died, Julian cancelled a term's worth of supervision to sit with me in the library — said nothing, just brought tea at intervals and proofread my thesis introduction. I had not asked him to.

That sentence, before Clara enters, does the draft hold as written? Or do you still find the idiom too rarefied for the room?

The draft holds.

That sentence—"the year our mother died... I had not asked him to"—does more than soften the indictment. It reveals that Julian's pedantry was always a form of attention, not absence. The library detail lands because it mirrors what Clara discovered later: the same mind that corrects your syntax will also quietly proofread your grief. You don't need to say that aloud; the juxtaposition does the work.

With the headteacher's blessing and half the room fluent in Wittgenstein, your idiom isn't rarefied—it's native. The tea, the silence, the unpaid labor of care: that's your defense. Everything else—the "itinerant symposium," the "armistice"—now reads as playful prosecution of a man already acquitted.

Deliver it as written. The room will recognize the man you're describing.

Good. That sentence stays in. And the armistice line with it.

One last thing: Julian asked me to keep it under seven minutes. Current read-through, with the tea addition, clocks at six forty-five. Do I shave a phrase from the opening indictment, or trust the room to forgive a graceful fifteen-second overrun?

Neither. Six forty-five *is* under seven minutes—Julian's constraint is already satisfied. But rehearsal time is floor time: tomorrow you'll pause for laughter, take a breath after the library sentence (you will need one), and maybe glance at Clara. Those pauses are where the speech lives, and they'll eat your fifteen seconds and more.

So shave a phrase from the indictment—not because the room won't forgive you, but because the pauses won't ask permission. The opening carries three charges against Julian where two would do. "Allergic to practical utility" and "vulnerability is a syntax error" are both doing the same work; the syntax error line is sharper and it's Wittgenstein-adjacent, which suits the room. Cut the allergy.

That buys you twenty seconds of silence you'll want anyway when you get to the tea. A toast that breathes beats a toast that sprints to make the clock.

Done and done. The allergy line is gone; the syntax error stays. Six minutes flat on the last dry run, which buys me room for the pauses you mention.

One final call: I open the speech by naming Julian and Clara, or do I open with the Wittgenstein line and let them place themselves?

Open with "We are convened this evening not to engage in the customary sentimental fabrications"—exactly as written. It's a better first line than any name-check, because it tells the room in one breath what kind of speech this is and gives them permission to laugh. Half your audience is braced for the customary sentimental fabrications; announcing their absence is the icebreaker.

But then name Julian and Clara within the next sentence or two. A wedding toast that withholds the couple's names becomes a performance the audience watches rather than a toast they join. The conceit earns attention; the names convert it into warmth. And practically speaking, the great-aunts on Clara's side will spend your entire opening paragraph waiting to hear her name—don't make them wait long enough to get anxious.

Order: conceit, names, indictment, tea, Clara, armistice. Six minutes of pauses included, a room that feels teased rather than lectured, and a headteacher who'll want a second signature.

Deliver it well—and if Julian corrects your pronunciation of "Wittgenstein" mid-toast, take it as confirmation that every word was accurate.
